title: The plant-system service desk
subtitle: Summer 1 • Explain how the parts work together
objective: Explain how roots, stem, leaves and flowers contribute to the life of a flowering plant.

sow.exactOutcome: Describe the job of each part of a plant.
sow.alignment: Chronological continuation of the supplied SOW. This lesson develops or reviews the named outcome; it does not claim an accreditation award.

priorLearning: Identify roots, stem, leaves and flower.
success: Match each main part to a useful job.
Distinguish mineral uptake from making sugars.

vocabulary.meaning: Take in a substance, such as water.
A substance needed in small amounts for growth.
A structure containing a young plant and food reserves.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one chosen pupil route; pencil; optional ruler; projector or offline HTML.
preparation: Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.
safety: Paper and screen route requires no biological handling.
practicalAlternative: All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.

misconceptions.correction: Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals; green parts make sugars using light.
misconceptions.check: Ask where sugars are made and where water enters.

misconceptions.claim: The stem only holds the flower.
misconceptions.correction: It supports parts and contains transport pathways.
misconceptions.check: Ask how root-absorbed water reaches leaves.

misconceptions.claim: Flowers exist only to look attractive.
misconceptions.correction: They take part in reproduction and can lead to seed formation.
misconceptions.check: Ask what a successfully fertilised flower can develop into.

access.supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
access.standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
access.stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.

sources.title: Department for Education: science programmes of study
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Year 3 plants, rocks, light and forces underpin the SOW. Accessible teaching models are adapted to the named lesson objective.

sources.title: Science and Plants for Schools: plant biology animations
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Scientific background for our original simplified diagrams: photosynthesis, growth and transport. No external animation is required or embedded.

sources.title: Science and Plants for Schools: water transport
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals; evaporation from leaves contributes to pulling water upwards. Phloem sugar transport is distinct.

slides.title: Can one plant part do every job?
body: Follow the work through the whole plant.
slides.notes: Do not anthropomorphise a service desk into intention: “jobs” means biological functions.

slides.title: Name the part before its function
slides.notes: 1 roots. 2 stem. 3 flowers take part in seed formation. Accept an emerging answer without requiring pollination detail.

slides.title: I connect entry to transport
body: Roots take in water and minerals.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “Water enters through the roots, but the leaves are higher up. I need a connecting pathway. Naming roots alone does not explain arrival at leaves.” Roots also anchor; arrows show selected water movement.

visual.title: Roots take in water and minerals
visual.description: Schematic root system absorbs water with dissolved mineral nutrients from soil; selected arrows then lead upwards through the stem. Soil is not eaten as ready-made food.

elements.text: The root system anchors the plant.

Water moves into
and through the plant.
Mineral nutrients are needed; they are not ready-made plant food.

slides.title: I distinguish materials from sugar-making
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “I see water arriving, but sugar-making also needs light and carbon dioxide from air. Soil is not a meal the roots eat.” Oxygen is also produced; the simplified diagram focuses on the inputs and sugar output.

visual.title: Green leaves make sugars
visual.description: Simplified photosynthesis input-output model: light provides energy; water and carbon dioxide from air are used to make sugars in green leaves. Only selected inputs and the sugar output are shown; oxygen is also produced.

elements.text: Roots supply water and minerals; the plant makes its sugars.

slides.title: I give flowers a biological function
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “A bright colour may help attract some pollinators, but it is not the whole function. I connect the flower with forming seeds.” Not every flower succeeds; not all flowers are bright or insect-pollinated.

visual.title: Flowers support the next generation
visual.description: Simplified flowering-plant sequence: a flower can develop into a fruit containing seeds after successful pollination and fertilisation. A seed can later germinate under suitable conditions. Not every flower successfully forms seeds.

elements.text: A simplified sequence; outcomes and timing vary.

slides.title: The service desk sorts the jobs
body: Connect each part to a function.
Explain one connection to another part.
slides.notes: W1: roots absorb/anchor; stem supports/transports; green leaves make sugars; flowers reproduction/seeds. Roles: explainer, evidence checker, connector. Rotate once.

table.caption: Functional matching; no live plant damage

slides.title: A repair must address the missing input
body: Say why an unrelated repair fails.
slides.notes: W2: E needs suitable light reaching leaves; more minerals alone cannot replace light. F needs transport through the stem. Never damage or deliberately shade a class plant to act out a fault.
slides.reveal: A connected system needs suitable inputs and working pathways.

slides.title: Which account explains plant nutrition?
body: Look for both making and absorbing.
slides.notes: Correct first option. If soil-food appears, revisit leafjob alongside rootjob.

options.text: Roots absorb water and minerals; green leaves make sugars using light.
Roots eat soil, so leaves have no role.
options.feedback: Minerals and soil are not the plant’s ready-made sugars.

options.text: Flowers pump all water from the soil.
options.feedback: Roots take in water, which travels through stem pathways.

slides.title: Choose your science route
slides.notes: Set ONE route. Use the same objective across routes. A successful connection includes an entry point and transport, or a photosynthesis input and sugar-making. Do not demand the full photosynthesis equation.

slides.title: Make your own evidence record
slides.notes: Use the same objective across routes. A successful connection includes an entry point and transport, or a photosynthesis input and sugar-making. Do not demand the full photosynthesis equation.

slides.title: Check what the evidence can show
body: Point to the clue you used.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Ask for a reason, not just a correct word. Use the same objective across routes. A successful connection includes an entry point and transport, or a photosynthesis input and sugar-making. Do not demand the full photosynthesis equation.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve the shared account
slides.notes: Listen to a selected pupil revision and visibly adopt a scientifically accurate contribution. Offer private, written or partner feedback.
slides.prompt: Which connection made our explanation stronger?
slides.reveal: Parts have different functions and work together; water uptake is different from making sugars.

slides.title: Keep the useful change
slides.notes: Shares review time. Name how a pupil contribution changed a label, method or conclusion. Do not rank pupils.
slides.reveal: Parts have different functions and work together; water uptake is different from making sugars.

slides.title: Three final checks
body: E1. Which part absorbs water from soil?
E2. Where do green plants make sugars using light?
E3. What do flowers help the plant do?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual evidence. Use the answer key and re-teach the specified misconception if needed.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence • Plant-system cards
pupilPages.intro: Use these biological function cards. The service cases are fictional; do not damage plants.

cards.title: A • Roots
cards.text: Anchor the plant. Absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients.

cards.title: B • Stem
cards.text: Supports leaves and flowers. Contains pathways transporting water and other substances.

cards.title: C • Green leaves
cards.text: Use light energy, water and carbon dioxide from air to make sugars.

cards.title: D • Flowers
cards.text: Take part in reproduction. After successful pollination and fertilisation, seeds can form.

cards.title: E • Service case
cards.text: A plant’s leaves are shaded by a box. Its roots still have water; the box prevents light reaching the leaves.

cards.title: F • Connection case
cards.text: Water has entered the roots. It still needs a pathway through the stem to reach the leaves.

blocks.prompt: W1. Choose two parts and explain how their jobs connect.
W2. Which input is missing in E? Why will extra minerals not replace it?

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Match useful jobs
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: roots / stem / leaves / flowers.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which part absorbs water from soil?
S2. Which part connects roots to leaves and transports water?
S3. Which green parts make sugars using light?
S4. Which parts take part in making seeds?
S5. Mineral nutrients are...
choices: Needed substances taken in with water.
Ready-made sugar meals eaten from soil.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write the service guide
pupilPages.intro: Use a part name, a function and a reason.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain how roots and stem help water reach a leaf.
M2. Explain why E needs light as well as water.
M3. Give two jobs of the stem.
M4. Correct “flowers only make the plant look colourful”.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Review a proposed repair
pupilPages.intro: A pupil says: “The shaded plant has water, so giving it twice as many minerals will replace the missing light.”

blocks.prompt: T1. Explain the mistake using card C.
T2. Propose a repair that addresses the missing input.
T3. Explain why roots alone cannot account for water reaching leaves.
T4. Must every flower become a seed-bearing fruit? Use a careful sentence.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. Which part absorbs water from soil?
E2. Where do green plants make sugars using light?
E3. What do flowers help the plant do?
R1. Which idea did you improve or defend? What evidence helped?
R2. What useful question would you investigate next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 roots. 2 stem. 3 flowers through reproduction and seed formation.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 roots take in water and stem carries it towards leaves; or stem supports leaves that receive light. Water entry roots; water transport stem; sugar-making green leaves; seed formation flowers. W2 light is missing; minerals cannot replace light energy.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: First option correct. The second treats soil as ready-made food; the third assigns root uptake to flowers.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 roots. S2 stem. S3 green leaves. S4 flowers. S5 needed substances taken in with water.

answers.label: M1–M4
answers.answer: M1 roots absorb water, which travels through pathways in the stem to leaves. M2 light energy is needed to make sugars from water and carbon dioxide; water alone is insufficient. M3 supports leaves/flowers and transports substances. M4 flowers take part in reproduction and can lead to seeds.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 minerals do not replace the light energy needed for photosynthesis. T2 allow suitable light to reach leaves while maintaining other needs. T3 a connected stem pathway carries water beyond the roots. T4 no; seed development depends on successful reproductive processes and other suitable conditions.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 roots. E2 green leaves and other photosynthetic green tissues; leaves sufficient for core. E3 reproduce/form seeds.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 7, We do 8, hinge 3, independent 12, review 3, exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the named stage time.
BUILD uses the supplied Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful contexts for older pupils. Supported, standard and stretch are selectable routes within the pathway.

Interactive We do: predict first, test against the controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. Shared W tasks offer the equivalent paper discussion. Animation is a teaching representation, not filmed experimental evidence.
Keep constructed evidence separate from actual class observations. Do not invent measurements or require internet research.
Secure core: four correct part-function links and one accurate connection. If a pupil says food comes from soil, contrast the labelled sugar output with root water/mineral uptake.

interactive.title: Choose the useful plant-system explanation
interactive.intro: Use service cards A–F. Predict a function or repair, reveal the diagram, then explain the connection.

steps.question: Water enters from soil. Which part takes it in?

choices.feedback: Roots absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients.
Petals are not the main soil-water entry route.

visual.title: Roots take in water and minerals
visual.description: Schematic root system absorbs water with dissolved mineral nutrients from soil; selected arrows then lead upwards through the stem. Soil is not eaten as ready-made food.

elements.text: The root system anchors the plant.

Water moves into
and through the plant.
Mineral nutrients are needed; they are not ready-made plant food.

steps.explanation: The stem then provides transport pathways towards leaves.

steps.question: In E, leaves receive no light. Will extra minerals replace light?

choices.feedback: Minerals do not supply the light energy required for photosynthesis.
Different requirements cannot simply replace one another.

visual.title: Green leaves make sugars
visual.description: Simplified photosynthesis input-output model: light provides energy; water and carbon dioxide from air are used to make sugars in green leaves. Only selected inputs and the sugar output are shown; oxygen is also produced.

steps.explanation: Restore suitable light; water and minerals remain necessary too.

steps.question: Which job explains flowers beyond appearance?

choices.text: They take part in reproduction and seed formation
choices.feedback: Successful fertilisation can lead to seeds.

choices.text: They are the only water-absorbing part
choices.feedback: Roots are the main entry point from soil.
